summary: The TRILL RBridge Channel mechanism from RFC 7178 allows typed messages between TRILL switches in the same campus and between switches and end stations on the same link. This proposed standard extends the RBridge Channel header so it can carry more information.

eli5.summary: TRILL switches have a private message line to talk to each other. This adds extra room in the envelope header of those messages so they can say more.

questions: what is trill rbridge channel header extension
what is stype in rbridge channel
how does trill secure rbridge channel messages
subtitle: Adds payload tunneling and security fields to the RBridge Channel header used between TRILL switches.

tldr.problem: The RBridge Channel in RFC 7178 carries typed messages between TRILL switches, but it has no standard way to tunnel arbitrary payloads or to authenticate and encrypt messages.
tldr.mechanism: A new RBridge Channel protocol (0x004) adds a header extension with a payload type (PType), a security type (SType), a suberror field and optional security information.
tldr.outcome: Messages can carry an Ethertyped payload or a whole Ethernet frame, and can be secured with IS-IS-based authentication, DTLS, or both. The document updates RFC 7178.

today: RFC 7978 is a Proposed Standard from September 2016 that updates RFC 7178. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Extend the RBridge Channel
sections.content:
TRILL switches, also called RBridges, can exchange typed messages through the RBridge Channel facility of RFC 7178. Between two RBridges in the same campus the message travels in a TRILL Data packet addressed by nickname. Between an RBridge and an end station on the same link, a native RBridge Channel message is used with no TRILL Header, addressed by MAC address.

RFC 7978 updates RFC 7178 with two optional facilities. The first is a standard way to tunnel payloads identified by Ethertype. The second is a way to secure RBridge Channel messages, with the RFC naming Pull Directory messages, address flush messages and port shutdown messages as example uses. If the extension is implemented, two payload types MUST be implemented, and where this document conflicts with RFC 7178, this document takes precedence.
sections.eli5: The switches already pass notes to each other. This lets the notes carry bigger things inside, and lets them be sealed so nobody else can read or fake them.

sections.title: The Extended Header
sections.content:
The RBridge Channel header starts with the RBridge-Channel Ethertype 0x8946, a 4-bit Channel Header Version (this document is based on version zero), a 12-bit Channel Protocol, a 12-bit Flags field and a 4-bit ERR field. The extension is itself a Channel protocol: the Protocol field is set to 0x004, so a remote RBridge's support can be learned from the protocols it advertises in its LSP.

Four new 4-bit fields follow. SubERR gives more detail about an error (it MUST be zero when ERR is zero). RESV4 MUST be sent as zero, and a non-zero value on receipt is an error. SType says what security is used, and PType says what the tunneled data is. Variable-length Security Information, empty when SType is zero, comes next, then the tunneled data.
sections.eli5: The envelope gets four new little boxes: one for what went wrong, one kept empty, one for how it is locked, and one for what is inside.

sections.title: Payload Types
sections.content:
The PType field takes these values: 0 reserved, 1 Null, 2 Ethertyped Payload, 3 Ethernet Frame, 4 to 14 unassigned and 15 reserved. If the extension is implemented, PType 1 and PType 2 with the RBridge-Channel Ethertype MUST be implemented. Other Ethertypes under PType 2, and PType 3, MAY be implemented. Handling of any message depends on local security and policy.

Null is for testing or for messages such as key negotiation where only security information is present. Any tunneled data is ignored.

Ethertyped payloads start with an Ethertype. The RBridge-Channel Ethertype nests another RBridge Channel message, typically to add authentication or encryption to it. The TRILL Ethertype (0x22F3) carries a TRILL Data packet, handled as if received on the port where the extended message arrived. The L2-IS-IS Ethertype (0x22F4) carries a TRILL IS-IS PDU, for example to speed up receipt of a link state PDU.

Ethernet Frame (PType 3) carries a frame as an end station would send it, without its own FCS. For non-Ethernet links such as PPP, a synthetic 48-bit link-local MAC address is built from 0xFEFF, the nickname of the TRILL switch used in Hellos on that port, and the Port ID.
sections.eli5: The note can carry nothing at all, another note, a whole letter from the TRILL mail system, or a copy of an ordinary network message, and the first line says which.

sections.title: Security Types
sections.content:
SType values are: 0 None, 1 IS-IS CRYPTO_AUTH-Based Authentication, 2 DTLS Pairwise Security, 3 Composite Security, 4 to 14 unassigned and 15 reserved. DTLS Pairwise (2) and Composite (3) are RECOMMENDED. The IS-IS option provides only authentication and no key negotiation, so its use is NOT RECOMMENDED.

SType 1 works like the IS-IS Authentication TLV. The Security Information holds a 4-bit RESV, a Size, a Key ID and the Authentication Data, covering the packet from just after the TRILL Header to just before the link trailer. The key used is derived from IS-IS keying material with HKDF-Expand-SHA256, using the string "Extended Channel" and the SType.

SType 2 places one or more DTLS records in the payload, with a negotiated DTLS version that MUST NOT be less than 1.2. Each record must fit in a single message. Implementations MUST support pre-shared keys; a two-byte psk_identity is read as an IS-IS Key ID. Keying uses priority 6 by default.

SType 3 combines both: DTLS records are wrapped in IS-IS-based authentication, which is checked first on receipt. That authenticates and encrypts the payload and also gives some authentication to the header and preceding addresses.

DTLS and Composite are meant for pairwise (known unicast) use. Multi-destination traffic can be sent by serial unicast, and a true group-keyed SType is planned for a separate document.
sections.eli5: There are four ways to seal the note: no seal, a signature stamp, a lock with a secret handshake, or both together. The RFC says the stamp alone is not good enough any more.

sections.title: Errors
sections.content:
Extension errors are reported using new ERR codes: 6 for an unknown or unsupported field value, 7 for authentication failure and 8 for an error in a nested RBridge Channel message. When ERR is 6, SubERR narrows it down: 1 non-zero RESV4, 2 unsupported SType, 3 unsupported PType, 4 unknown Key ID, 5 unsupported Ethertype with PType 2, 6 unsupported authentication algorithm for SType 1, and 7 non-zero SubERR with a zero ERR field.

If a secured message nests another RBridge Channel message and that nested message produces an error reply, the reply SHOULD also be nested in an extended message with the same type of security, with ERR set to 8.
sections.eli5: If something is wrong with the note, the reply has a number saying what, and a second number saying exactly which part.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The extension can help and hurt. It offers optional authentication and encryption for messages that lack their own security. But tunneling more payload types, and tunneling them to and from end stations, can increase risk. Processing decapsulated payloads is a place where an implementation SHOULD NOT be liberal in what it accepts, and local policy SHOULD generally accept only the payload types needed, with adequate security.

If IS-IS authentication is not in use, IS-IS CRYPTO_AUTH keying material would not normally be available, which the RFC reads as a decision by the operator that no security is needed. General security considerations are in RFC 7178 and RFC 6325.
sections.eli5: A bigger mailbox means more kinds of mail can arrive, so the switches should only open the kinds they expect and only when properly sealed.

fields.name: CHV
fields.desc: Channel Header Version; this document uses version zero.

fields.name: Channel Protocol
fields.desc: Indicates the header extension is present.

fields.name: SubERR
fields.desc: Further detail when ERR is set; zero when ERR is zero.

fields.name: SType
fields.desc: Type of security information in use.

fields.name: PType
fields.desc: Payload type of the tunneled data.

items.label: None
items.desc: No security services; Security Information has length zero.

items.label: DTLS Pairwise Security
items.desc: DTLS records in the payload; RECOMMENDED.

items.label: Composite Security
items.desc: DTLS wrapped in IS-IS-based authentication; RECOMMENDED.
